items.title: Toll Brothers underwrites lots for tomorrow's market, not yesterday's
items.description: As margins for error narrow in homebuilding’s land rules of engagement, boundaries between strategy and tactics have begun to blur. As slower sales , weaker demand, moderating sales prices and declining margins continue to look for a stabilizing floor, homebuilding land acquisition decision-makers now typically take a more discriminating, granular and real-time look at each deal to ensure it measures up to indefinitely challenging selling conditions. While many builders contend with land bought in a stronger market that is now becoming a liability, Toll Brothers has spent the last few years raising its underwriting bar and tightening it further. That approach is shaping more than what the builder will pay for land. It is influencing where Toll considers building, how it structures deals and where it finds opportunity as competitors reassess older purchases. Rob Paul, Texas and Arkansas group president, and Dustin Bowersett, VP of land acquisition for Toll’s Central Florida division, elaborated on the company’s land strategy during a session last week at the HousingWire Homebuilder Summit , moderated by longtime Wall Street housing analyst Dan Oppenheim. That strategy follows a clear thread. Stricter underwriting, a focus on the best locations, selectivity when sellers won’t budge on price and an emphasis on trusted relationships with land sellers all show how Toll Brothers tries to stay out ahead of a slowing market rather than react to it. Toll Brothers raises the bar for new land Toll Brothers began reassessing its underwriting criteria for evaluating land a few years ago. At the time, lots traded aggressively on the expectation that homes would sell quickly and at high margins, particularly in many high-growth Sun Belt markets. Paul noted that Toll Brothers' land committee is getting much stricter when evaluating deals. As market conditions tightened, the company course-corrected its approach and began scoring land based on a combination of gross margin and internal rate of return (IRR). “The increase of that threshold and making the underwriting more strict over the course of the last couple of years has put us in a position where, should the market turn, we retain some value,” Paul said. This underwriting criteria also considers recent sales performance, while discounting sales performance experienced during the spring, since conditions have worsened since then. “The sales in the last…60 to 90 days absolutely drive decisions. We’re starting to look at what’s happened in the last couple of weeks,” Paul said. Essentially, Toll Brothers expects its newer land purchases to pencil even if the market worsens, because they were completed under higher hurdle-rate standards. The finer point is that the market has changed enough to demand a shift in mindset, with Paul arguing that builders should underwrite the conditions they are likely to face, not the ones they operated through earlier in the year. The Toll Brothers “main and main” advantage Since its inception, Toll Brothers has abided by a “Main-and-Main” philosophy, characterized by purchasing lots in the best locations, i.e. Main Street. This strategy makes sense for Toll Brothers, which has the highest average sales price of any public homebuilder in the country, coming in at roughly $1 million nationally. Bowersett noted that, while Toll Brothers’ Central Florida division sells homes between about $350,000 and $5 million, the vast majority of the division’s volume falls in the $850,000 to $1.3 million range. The bulk of those transactions are domestic move-up buyers, but many are wealthy foreign buyers from Latin America. Regardless of where they come from, they seek top-tier locations in neighborhoods with good schools and a high quality of life. Another reason validates Toll Brothers' focus on Main-and-Main locations. Many fringe areas are now struggling as demand for more affordably priced homes softens or stalls. When buyers are plentiful and demand is high, outlying locations can look like smart bets. However, when that demand thins, the gap between prime and peripheral land can widen quickly. Bowersett pointed to Polk County, Florida, a growing suburban and exurban county located between Orlando and Tampa as an example. During the post-COVID building boom, builders aggressively pursued peripheral land in Polk County. Production builders posted strong absorption rates, developers offered relatively attractive lot pricing and deal structures were easier to negotiate. Now, as population growth and demand in Polk County moderate, that submarket has lost some luster. In hindsight, Toll Brothers’s decision not to pull the trigger on opportunities there proved to be prudent. “We decided not to. We stayed in our core markets, and if you look right now…the lots are essentially worthless in some instances,” Bowersett noted. Peripheral markets nationwide mirror Polk County's dynamics. “The fringe is what gets hurt first, period,” Paul said. “When there are fewer buyers, the market gets a little tough. There’s a flight to quality.” Paul said buyer psychology helps explain the phenomenon. Even when homes are comparable on paper, buyers weigh the risk of being wrong about where they buy. “Buyers don’t want to feel stupid. They don’t want to feel dumb. They don’t want to feel like they’re making a mistake,” he said. “There’s safety in a community that’s already half-built-out. There’s safety in a community that has 10 home sites left.” That preference gives established communities an edge over new fringe developments, reinforcing how Toll Brothers thinks about land. A softer market isn’t lowering demand equally across the board. Instead, demand often remains strongest in central, established locations, leaving builders with outer-ring exposure with a weaker hand to play. Land sellers concede on terms before they cut price Despite a more challenging sales environment, Paul said land sellers are mostly standing pat on lot prices. Toll Brothers

items.title: CoStar wants faster Homes.com growth, is shifting sales into the field
items.description: CoStar Group may have recorded its 62nd consecutive quarter of double-digit annual revenue growth in the third quarter of 2026, but CEO and founder Andy Florance wants more. Company-wide, net new bookings came in at $37 million for the quarter, below expectations. “Our renewal rates remained high, but with a growing multibillion-dollar subscription base, we need to continue to grow high ROI sales force headcount,” Florence, the 2026 HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said on his firm’s Q3 2026 earnings call with investors and analysts Tuesday night. “Our sales team met with hundreds of thousands of clients and prospects, but they lack the scale to reach the hundreds of thousands of additional prospects we have.” According to Florance, CoStar currently has roughly 2,000 sales professionals on staff, down roughly 10% compared to a year ago. Looking ahead, Florance said CoStar is focused on making changes to the Homes.com sales team, which originally launched with a large, centralized inside sales team based out of the company’s headquarters in Richmond, Virginia. “We'll continue to build the Richmond team, but we are shifting most of our growth effort to the field sales professionals with prior real estate and sales experience in our top cities,” Florance said. “Field reps who meet with clients face-to-face are, on average, much more productive than inside sales and having visited prospects and clients with our home field sales teams at the agents' open houses and offices.” For the quarter, Homes.com generated $7 million of annualized net new bookings, despite reducing inside sales reps from a peak of 655 a year ago to 267 today. “When we demo Homes membership to an agent, we consistently achieved close rates above 40%,” Florance said. “The objective is more demos and expanding our field sales team is how we get in front of more agents.” This performance comes a little over six months after activist investor campaigns called on CoStar to divest its Homes.com assets. Overall, CoStar’s residential real estate segment generated $460 million in revenue, up from $373 million a year ago. In total, the company generated $952 million in revenue for the quarter, up 14% annually. Additionally, CoStar Group reported $74 million in net income, up $105 million from a year prior. As CoStar looks to continue to maintain its profitability, executives noted that the firm had achieved $150 million in cost efficiencies so far this year, noting the ongoing expense reviews have identified potential additional savings of at least $200 million, which the firm expects to realize over the next 12 to 18 months. Acquisitions performing well CoStar also called out the performance of some of its recent acquisitions during the call, noting that Matterport’ s subscription revenue was up 11%, direct sales bookings was up 14% and new enterprise customers was up 46% year-over-year during the quarter. Executives added that they expect Matterport to be profitable by the end of 2027. In addition to this, executives also highlighted Zonda ’s performance. CoStar closed its $815 million acquisition of Zonda in late August. According to CoStar, Zonda's pro forma third quarter revenue was $42 million, roughly 75% of which was subscription, which grew 4% despite a difficult new homes market. The company also announced its agreement to acquire survey-grade aerial imagery program Vexcel Group for roughly $730 million in cash. CoStar said it expects the deal, which will be funded with cash on hand and CoStar’s existing revolving credit facility, to close during the first quarter of 2027. Vexcel operates a global aerial imagery and geospatial data program that captures more than 60 million images a year across millions of square kilometers. Its coverage spans more than 45 countries, 320 major global metros and 99.6% of the U.S. population. The firm refreshes major U.S. metros as often as three times per year and flies disaster zones within 24 hours of an event for catastrophe assessment and response. “Rapid technology advances in aerial photography and lidar are enabling Vexcel to produce extremely high-resolution images and survey-grade measurements of land, houses, office buildings, industrial properties, retail properties, apartment buildings, construction sites and other infrastructure in the built environment,” Florance said in the announcement. Following closing, Vexcel will continue to operate its data program under the Vexcel brand and serve its existing customers and partners. CEO Erik Jorgensen and the current leadership team are expected to remain in place. For CoStar, which owns Homes.com, Apartments.com , LoopNet and other marketplaces, Vexcel’s imagery and derived data could support richer listing content, more accurate property attributes, improved lead qualification and new data products for lenders, investors and government clients. items.title: NYC office-to-apartment mega project resumes after near disaster
items.description: Crews have finished lifting the sagging floors at the former Pfizer headquarters, the largest office-to-apartment conversion in city history. A July structural failure forced evacuations across seven Midtown East blocks and, for a fleeting moment, threw a menacing cloud over a nationwide push to turn empty offices into housing. Two columns buckled at the 1,600-unit conversion, which touched off inspections citywide, and stop-work orders followed. Concern spread nationwide , generating questions over cost, safety and design in adaptive reuse of decades-old office buildings. Cities from Washington to Los Angeles have bet that converting vacant offices can add housing faster than ground-up construction. New York leads that push, and others emulate its tax breaks and zoning changes. Mayor Zohran Mamdani inherited a conversion pipeline of about 12,000 units and has embraced it as a pillar of his own housing affordability pitch. Mamdani has leaned into commercial-to-residential conversion as part of a multi-pronged approach to increasing housing supply. More than 40 other conversions are underway or planned citywide, adding more than 14,000 homes. The city has issued 16 new building permits for conversions since July. The pipeline is holding steady. State tax law's 467-m program offers a property tax exemption of up to 35 years for rental conversions that include affordable units. A June 30 deadline this year locked in the tax break. Nate Bliss, founder of Latent Urban Ventures , told HousingWire TBD that applications are picking back up. "There's a lot of activity of people trying to get their projects moving in the next six months, so they can meet the June 30, 2028, deadline" for a 30-year break for projects that start by mid-2028, Bliss said. "We still have a long way to go and plenty of office stock to convert." Fixing the conversion This past summer, two columns buckled on the 21st floor of the Pfizer building make-over, under floor area recently added to the top of the building. The project's structural engineer blamed missing steel reinforcement, rather than design. Inspectors found no imminent structural dangers. New York City Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said in a social media video that the tower "has remained stable" and poses no danger to the public. Developer engineers designed a plan to jack up floors above the affected area, which had dropped about six inches, Tigani said. Senior department engineers and an independent third-party firm vetted the plan before approval. “That plan has moved forward and is now complete,” Tigani said. Some lower-floor work has been allowed to continue. Upper floors remain limited to housekeeping and repairs tied to the fix. "We will not allow work to proceed unless we are confident that all could be done safely," Tigani said. MetroLoft and David Werner Real Estate Investments lead the project, which includes about 400 affordable, rent-stabilized apartments. Other projects move ahead Inspections of 180 sites turned up 65 violations across 38 locations. They led to 18 partial stop-work orders and one full halt. Work has resumed at some of those sites. Deals continue. In September, Capstone Equities and BH3 Management landed a $208 million loan through Northwind Group to convert upper floors of a three-year-old, never-occupied 24-story downtown Brooklyn tower into 239 apartments. BH3's Adam Falk told The Wall Street Journal the conversion should take 18 to 20 months instead of four to five years for new development. Related More: Affordable Housing Construction

items.title: Open Real Estate gains momentum as independent brokerages sign on
items.description: For Donny Samson, the CEO and principal broker of Virginia-based RealTrends Verified Samson Properties , the decision to have his firm join Open Real Estate as one of the first participating brokerages was a no-brainer. “I have been pretty outspoken over the last year or two about consumers having the ability to see all the options,” Samson said. “In the [D.C.-Maryland-Virginia] market, there are a lot of listings that are not fully visible to the public and that has been a frustrating process for them. I’ve just been so passionate about making every listing available for everybody to see, as it is the best for sellers and buyers, that I think that caught the attention of the founders.” Samson said AGNT CEO and 2026 HousingWire Vanguard award winner Leo Pareja , who he considers a friend in the industry, reached out to discuss Open Real Estate and that before Pareja was done explaining the idea, he was ready to sign on. “I don’t want to be in a world where three years from now sellers are going to have to list with seven agents in order for their listings to get in front of buyers,” Samson said. Getting in at the ground level Launched on Monday by AGNT, (the parent company of eXp Realty and NextHome franchises), HomeServices of America , Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group , all RealTrends Verified brokerages, Open Real Estate is a “national residential real estate data-sharing initiative.” The founders of the initiative have specified that this is not a national MLS nor are they seeking to replace local MLSs, but rather an initiative seeking to “streamline the distribution of property information, expand access to housing inventory and support a more open, competitive housing marketplace.” Samson said he is proud that his firm is one of the first participating brokerages. “I feel honored,” he said. “I feel like we are on the right side of this issue.” While not one of the four initial participating brokerages, RealTrends Verified GameChanger Iron Valley Real Estate announced it had signed on to Open Real Estate just hours after the news broke. “When I saw it come across, I jumped on it right away and spoke with my business partner, and we felt like it was the right thing for us to do,” Rob Cleapor, the CEO of Iron Valley Real Estate, said. “We believe in an open, cooperative marketplace because we feel that it gives the consumer more opportunities. We felt like it was the right thing to do for the industry and for the consumer.” Cleapor added that he hopes Open Real Estate preserves the inter-brokerage cooperation the U.S. housing market is known for as it creates a better transaction experience for consumers and it allows buyers and sellers to work with the agent they want, not the agent with the access to the largest private network. “I don’t think buyers should ever have to sacrifice their ability to choose an agent based on trust, service and expertise,” Cleapor said. “That is what I’m really hoping comes out of this.” Antitrust red flags But in a post-Sitzer/Burnett environment , cooperation among real estate brokerages doesn’t come without some concern regarding antitrust enforcement. For Samson though, this was not a concern. “It sounds silly, but when you hear that the four companies that have been so vocal about this issue are the founding members, and they want everyone to be included, I felt like they wouldn’t be out talking to me about it if they hadn’t run everything through with their lawyers and dotted their ‘Is’ and crossed their ‘Ts.’ I understand that antitrust is a touchy subject, but I can’t imagine how something we are trying to do for the betterment of the consumer experience could be something that could be litigiously come after,” he said. Cleapor added that cooperation among competitors has always been at the center of the U.S. real estate industry. “Our fiduciary duty is always for the consumer,” Cleapor said. “So, I think, as long as everyone that is involved with this — all of the brokers, owners and brokerages — always have the best interests of the consumers at heart, I don’t think we have to worry about antitrust laws.” Open for opportunities Although it is still early days for Open Real Estate, which is expected to launch in Q1 2027 , Samson said he is hopeful that all other brokerages join the initiative. “In my perfect world everybody would be singing from the same sheet of music, and we’d all be reading the same book,” Samson said. “Open Real Estate is a system that was created by agents with the mindset that we know what information we need and that we are putting it in one depository that will make it easier for us to disperse to MLSs, portals and any other site that needs good, clean data, not fragmented data from some brokerages and not others. This is what would be best for buyers and sellers.” Samson said it would be easy for brokerages to stick their head in the sand and pretend that everything is fine, but he believes it is important to be part of an initiative that he feels is working to create a better experience for consumers and agents. “Samson Properties wants to be part of the solution and part of creating a better environment moving forward," Samson said. Cleapor added that while every brokerage needs to make the right choice for their business, culture, values and goals, if they want to preserve a market where buyers can see all available inventory and sellers understand their marketing options, joining Open Real Estate should be something they consider. “The public is seeing a lot of negative in the real estate space right now, from brokerages and MLSs suing each other, to high mortgage rates and a slow market, but I hope with Open Real Estate we can create a positive message for the consumer, so they feel confident in the real estate industry and that agents have their best interest in mind,” Cleapor said. Related More: Clear Cooperation Donny Samson Samson Properties

items.title: DWS Must Sell: Key UK, Ireland, Netherlands Assets
items.description: German giant Deutsche Bank ’s asset manager, DWS Group , is looking to sell properties to generate liquidity for investors in its €4.3B Grundbesitz Europa real estate fund after restricting redemptions. The German fund manager said it would initially pay just 10% of redemption requests falling due, under a restriction taking effect from 27 October and intended to give DWS more time to raise cash through orderly property sales. Unsplash/Sean Pollock DWS needs to sell properties in its portfolio after capping redemptions. The fund had €342.8M in liquid assets at the end of September, against a net asset value of €4.3B and a property portfolio valued at €6.3B, according to its most recent fact sheet. Its holdings span 63 properties across Europe, including offices, residential buildings and retail assets, with some held directly and others through property companies. The portfolio includes several substantial UK assets, alongside residential property in Ireland and offices in Amsterdam. Their presence on the fund's balance sheet does not mean they are being marketed for sale, and DWS has not disclosed which buildings it may seek to dispose of, but they are all options for the fund. DWS said in a statement that the redemption restriction would allow the fund to “generate liquidity through orderly sales processes and potentially achieve appropriate returns again in the future.” The cap is permitted for up to 12 months but can be reviewed and adjusted or lifted early. It follows a prolonged period of withdrawals from German open-ended property funds as higher interest rates and pressure on property values have challenged a model that allows investors to quickly redeem holdings while the underlying assets can take months or years to sell. According to DWS’ reported values and floor areas, its holdings across three key European markets include 21.2% in the UK, 3.6% in the Netherlands and 2.9% in Ireland. The UK S5 International Quarter, Stratford Directly held Value: €348.6M Size: 511,100 SF The Stratford office tower is one of the fund's largest UK holdings. Completed in 2018 in the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park business district, the 20-storey building is let long-term to the UK's Financial Conduct Authority. The Northcliffe, Tudor Street Directly held Value: €214.5M Size: 187,600 SF The former Daily Mail headquarters and printing works is a Grade II-listed office building renamed The Northcliffe. DWS said more than 80% of its space is let, with some leases running to 2038, and it reports rental levels above its business-plan assumptions. The building has undergone energy-efficiency improvements and holds a BREEAM Outstanding rating. Peckham Place, south London Held 100% through a company Value: €55.6M Size: 90,500 SF The residential building on Queen's Road, Peckham, is held through Peckham Place, which the DWS fund wholly owns. 2 St Peter's Square, Manchester Directly held Value: €95.4M Size: 165K SF The Manchester city centre office building was developed by Mosley Street Ventures, a business owned by Betfred founders the Done family. The freehold of 2 St Peter’s Square was sold to a fund controlled by DWS early in construction for £100M in 2015. Palace Exchange and Palace Gardens, Enfield Directly held Value: €69M combined Size: 424K SF DWS owns two shopping centres in Enfield, north London: Palace Exchange, valued at €39.8M, and Palace Gardens, valued at €29.3M. Circle Square, Manchester Held 63.7% through a company Value: €129.9M Size: 198K SF These purpose-built student accommodation blocks were acquired as part of a portfolio of Vita Student assets for around £600M in August 2019 on behalf of its real estate funds. Ireland 6 Upper Glenageary Road, Dún Laoghaire Held 100% through a company Value: €186.5M Size: 344K SF The residential development on Upper Glenageary Road is held through Grundbesitz Europa ICAV, a company the fund wholly owns. The 214 rental units were acquired for €108M in 2019, several months before scheme completion. The Netherlands Rivierstaete, Amsterdam Directly held Value: €177.3M Size: 313K SF Rivierstaete is a mixed-use office and residential complex on the Amstel, comprising the RiverSide and CitySide office sections alongside a residential block. DWS says it underwent a comprehensive modernisation completed in 2018 and is let on a long-term basis to a major international communications and marketing services business. Huys Azië, Amsterdam Directly held Value: €47.8M Size: 92K SF The eight-storey office building at Jollemanhof overlooks the IJ waterfront and includes 120 underground parking spaces. DWS says a Dutch legal advisory firm signed a new lease in 2025 with a term of around six years. items.title: Hof Wonen Acquires 251 Social Homes In The Hague
items.description: Housing corporation Hof Wonen has acquired 251 to-be-built social rental homes in Soza, a new large-scale, mixed-use urban project being developed by Vorm in The Hague. The deal, which follows Achmea Real Estate forward-purchasing 517 rental homes in the project on behalf of PME Pension, unlocks the start of the project’s first phase, the residential complex. The project will create a new urban commercial and residential neighborhood in the Central Innovation District. Hof Wonen/Vivid A rendering of the Soza skyline and canal in The Hague Located at the site of the former Ministry of Social Affairs office complex, opposite the Laan Van NOI train station in the Bezuidenhout district, Soza will offer a total of 1,194 houses for rent and for sale, as well as an office tower, commercial units and green spaces. Following the finalization of the zoning plan and environmental permit in June, the development has advanced significantly toward implementation, with initial residential completions targeted for 2030. Financial terms concerning the Hof Wonen transaction were not disclosed. Thirty percent of Soza's housing will be designated as social housing, and a minimum of 20% will be classified as midrange market, in response to The Hague’s pressing need for affordable housing. The remaining residential space will fall under the private sector segment. The rental units within the residential tower include studio, two- and three-room apartments ranging from 30 square meters to 90 square meters. Next to the residential units, Soza will offer commercial units suitable for a number of tenants, including supermarkets, bicycle repair stores, healthcare services, fitness facilities and hospitality. Approximately 24,000 square meters of multitenant floor space will be available to let in the office building, with lots ranging from 1,100 square meters on the ground floor to a minimum of 700 square meters on the seventh floor. Constructed from timber, the office building is aiming for a BREEAM -NL Excellent certification and will house a rooftop park, cafe, restaurant and other amenities. The Haaglanden region in the Netherlands continues to grapple with a housing shortage, equal to 6.7% of its existing stock and above the national average of 4.8%, according to research from ABF. An additional 25,000 homes would have to be created to reach the 2% policy target, according to housing and rental property platform Pararius. The gap in the rental housing market in The Hague is especially noticeable in the social sector, as there are approximately 90,000 active house hunters and only 8,000 social rental homes available, according to the collaborative housing association Sociale Verhuurders Haaglanden. As a result, fewer people are able to secure a social rental home, with the success rate falling from 13% in 2023 to 10.4% in 2024, and to just 5.8% for applicants responding to advertised homes, according to ABF. items.title: Hedge Fund Leases Top Floors At 70 Hudson Yards
items.description: The penthouse office of the next Hudson Yards skyscraper is off the market. Related Cos . and Oxford Properties Group have secured a tenant for the top two floors of 70 Hudson Yards , a $2.5B, under-construction office tower on the West Side of Manhattan, Oxford Head of U.S. Sara Queen said Tuesday at the Urban Land Institute's fall meeting in Miami Beach. Courtesy of Related Cos. 70 Hudson Yards, a 1.4M SF office building set to serve as Deloitte's future headquarters Queen didn't name the company that signed the lease, but she said it leased roughly 60K SF and that rent in the deal is $324 per SF. “That is a big number,” Queen said onstage. “What we are seeing is, for the best space in New York, there is a tremendous amount of interest. It is hard to find it.” Qube Research and Technologies, a London-based quantitative hedge fund with $50B of assets under management , was identified in Avison Young 's third-quarter office report this month as a new tenant at 70 Hudson Yards. The deal, which Commercial Observer first reported , didn't specify which floors or the rent, and Avison Young pegged the lease at 52K SF. A person familiar with the deal confirmed that QRT is taking the top two floors of 70 Hudson Yards, which are each roughly 30K SF. Spokespeople for Oxford and Related declined to comment. The lease is one of the most expensive ever signed for U.S. office space, but it's not quite a record. Related claimed that crown 2 miles northeast of 70 Hudson Yards at its other in-progress office tower, 625 Madison Ave . Another hedge fund, Castle Hook Partners, is paying $375 per SF for the top two floors at that building, which is expected to open in 2029. Related and Oxford landed a $1.6B construction loan for 70 Hudson Yards at the end of 2025 from Wells Fargo , Bank of America and Standard Chartered PLC, and they sold a $412.6M stake in the project to the Kuwait Investment Authority . Deloitte plans to move its North American headquarters to the 1.4M SF tower, which is expected to finish construction in 2028. It signed a 22-year, 807K SF lease in 2025, committing to pay more than $2.6B over the course of the deal with rents close to $150 per SF, according to CompStak. Designed by Gensler and Roger Ferris + Partners, 70 Hudson Yards is projected to be New York's first all-electric, carbon-neutral office building, Related said earlier this year. QRT is the second confirmed tenant in the project, but the person with knowledge of its deal said more leases are in the works. It is relocating from the 64th floor of 50 Hudson Yards , also developed and owned by Related and Oxford. That tower was the largest by square footage in the first phase of the $25B megaproject, which is essentially fully leased as competition for the best office buildings in Manhattan has heated up this year. The developers have secured approval and $2B in public financing for the residential-focused Phase 2 decking over the remaining rail yard, although Mayor Zohran Mamdani is reportedly considering canceling the subsidy , which Related has said the project needs to advance. When Related and Oxford broke ground last year on 70 Hudson Yards, it was the largest office project to start construction in the U.S. since the pandemic. A group of New York developers, including Related at 625 Madison, have followed suit as tenants demonstrate they will pay historically high rents for new space. Available office space has rapidly dwindled in Manhattan, which is on pace for the most active year of leasing since 2000 . On an earnings call last week, SL Green CEO Marc Holliday, whose REIT is developing an 850K SF tower at 346 Madison Ave ., said new buildings in Manhattan are being underwritten with midpoint average rents between $240 and $270 per SF. “Those are big rents and they're rents that are being signed up, they're rents that I think the tenant community has come to expect in order to cover costs, cover interest and cover profit,” Holliday said last Thursday. “So I think that is the new mark.” Chloe Gallivan contributed reporting from Miami. items.title: CoStar Acquiring Aerial Imaging Firm Vexcel For $730M
items.description: CoStar Group is taking to the skies with its latest acquisition. But after announcing the purchase of an aerial imaging company along with its third-quarter earnings, the commercial real estate tech giant's stock is hitting some turbulence. Pixabay/Hotshoe55 Arlington, Virginia-based CoStar has reached a $730M all-cash deal to buy Vexcel, which uses manned aircraft and proprietary imaging technology to collect tens of millions of high-resolution aerial photographs a year across 45 countries. CoStar for years has used fleets of cars to capture photographs of buildings for its vast property database. It plans to complement that with Vexcel's aerial photography and use artificial intelligence to "recognize and extract information and features from them," CEO Andy Florance said Tuesday on CoStar's earnings call. "It is clearly aligned with our mission of digitizing the world's real estate with an incredible ability to leverage AI to create proprietary real estate data of durable value," Florance added. Vexcel brought in $140M in revenue over the last 12 months, up 30% year-over-year, with a six-person sales team, Florance said. He said CoStar can supercharge that growth by expanding Vexcel's sales workforce with CoStar's own 2,000-person sales team. Erik Jorgensen is expected to continue as CEO of Vexcel, which will keep operating its data program and serve its customers under its own brand, CoStar's press release says. The deal is slated to close early next year. "By joining CoStar Group, we gain the scale, technology, and resources to broaden our reach, accelerate innovation, and deliver even greater value to customers worldwide," Jorgensen said in the release. The deal continues CoStar's decades-long strategy of growing through acquisitions. In August, it closed the previously announced acquisition of housing data provider Zonda for $815M. The company's biggest acquisition in recent years was the $1.6B deal to acquire 3D imaging company Matterport that closed in February 2025 . During a question-and-answer session with analysts, Florance compared the Vexcel acquisition to Matterport for the way it will continue to operate as its own company. "In terms of exclusivity, I think this works a little bit like Matterport," Florance said. "Matterport continues to grow as a standalone product, but because it's a combined entity with CoStar, the team at Matterport does a great job in making sure their products are responsive to the needs of our product areas, whether it be apartments, LoopNet [or] homes." Matterport's subscription revenue grew 11% year-over-year in the third quarter, and CoStar expects it to be profitable by the end of next year, Florance said. CoStar's overall revenue rose 14% year-over-year to $952M, and its net income totaled $74M, according to its earnings statement, released after markets closed Tuesday. The company raised its full-year guidance for revenue and earnings from its second-quarter estimates. But Wall Street reacted negatively to CoStar's earnings report, with the company's share price plunging by more than 13% Wednesday. Its stock is down 65% over the last year. Investors appeared to be spooked by CoStar's decline in annualized net new bookings, which totaled $37M last quarter, compared to $84M a year earlier. According to Investing.com , analysts BTIG and Jefferies cut their price targets for CoStar following Tuesday's earnings report. Florance said net new bookings came in below his expectations due to "economic headwinds and slower-than-expected sales force growth." items.title: For Fed, politics impossible to avoid in pre-midterm FOMC
items.description: Monetary policy For Fed, politics impossible to avoid in pre-midterm FOMC By Kyle Campbell CloseText About Kyle twitter ByKyleCampbell Published October 28, 2026, 6:00 a.m. EDT | Updated October 28, 2026, 3:23 p.m. EDT 7 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman. Federal Reserve Board Processing Content Key insight: The midterm elections are likely shaping market expectations about the Federal Open Market Committee's policy more than the decision itself. But the political implications are still consequential. Expert quote: "The Fed stresses very much its own independence and its political independence. They wouldn't want to be seen, for instance, raising rates and hurting the administration, the economy in general." — Dan North, senior economist for Allianz Trade Americas The Federal Open Market Committee is broadly expected to keep interest rates unchanged despite signs that inflation is worsening. More than 90% of federal funds futures contracts are pricing in no change to the benchmark rate after Wednesday's meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool, despite nearly 84% of the market anticipating at least one 25 basis point increase before the end of the year. There are several dynamics driving this sentiment. Some economists question the effectiveness of the Fed's policy tools in the current environment. Others are simply following the latest guidance from FOMC participants — outdated as it might be. Then there's the politics of it all. Because of next week's midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years, some analysts believe the Fed will be reluctant to deliver a surprise hike, lest it be seen as putting its thumb on the scale of public sentiment. "We've got the midterms coming up next week, so that is a little bit of a delicate situation," said Dan North, senior economist for Allianz Trade Americas. "I think the Fed will take the position of doing nothing, because if they were to raise rates, that would raise questions about political favor, somehow, on the Federal Reserve. They want to avoid that." President Donald Trump — who stands to lose his governing majority and face myriad congressional investigations into his administration should Democrats take one or both of the houses — is always ready to criticize the central bank for what he sees as partisan policy actions. But North said the issue is not Trump-specific. He would expect the Fed to steer clear of the political fray under any administration. Not because a single rate hike would change the economic outlook dramatically in one week — such changes take months to take effect — but because of the optics. "The Fed stresses very much its own independence and its political independence," North said. "They wouldn't want to be seen, for instance, raising rates and hurting the administration, the economy in general." The historical record on FOMC activity ahead of midterm elections is thin and the results are mixed. Since 1954, the committee has convened in October or early November ahead of a midterm election 11 times, according to data on committee votes maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Those meetings have resulted in three rate hikes, four rate decreases and four instances of no change. For all federal elections — including presidential cycles as well as midterms — the results are similar: the FOMC dropped rates 10 times, raised them six and held them steady nine. There were also 10 election cycles in which the Fed did not vote immediately before ballots were cast but instead, met in late September and again shortly after the election. More recently, rate increases directly before federal elections have become increasingly rare. The committee has approved just one pre-election hike since 1980: a 75 basis point increase directly before the last set of midterms in 2022. That jumbo rate hike was the fourth consecutive three-quarter-point increase by the FOMC, its sixth raise in as many meetings and part of an overall policy tightening campaign that saw the federal funds rate increase more than 5 percentage points in a single year. This is emblematic of other pre-election rate increases. Such moves have tended to be part of hiking cycles that span several consecutive meetings. Read more: As fintechs nab bank charters, what's happening to BaaS? Overheated data center knocked 23 credit unions offline Chris Britt still says banking is broken, but Chime can fix it Credit unions bulk up a business that banks long dominated In theory, the Fed could be at the beginning of such a cycle. The FOMC raised rates in September, most committee members expected to raise at least once more this year and the Fed's primary concern at the moment — persistently high inflation — appears to be trending in the wrong direction . The consumer price index was up 3.7% year over year in September, with input prices rising even more sharply . "All in all, economic data suggest that there is no good reason for the Fed to delay tightening monetary policy," said Jerry Tempelman, former senior analyst at the New York Fed and current vice president of economic and fixed income research at Mutual of America Capital Management. But recent commentary from Fed officials suggests the current tightening campaign might move in fits and starts. In a speech earlier this month, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said he supported the hike last month as a way of shoring up the Fed's credibility, rather than an outright effort to crush inflation. "This was an important step to ensure longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored and to validate the public's confidence that we will achieve our 2% inflation objective in a timely manner," Jefferson said. items.description: Servicing Post-2022 loans drive 43% of foreclosure starts; act early By Colin McNamara Published October 28, 2026, 5:43 a.m. EDT | Updated October 28, 2026, 4:52 p.m. EDT 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: Mortgage servicers risk rising defaults if they fail to spot early borrower distress. Supporting Data: 43% of September's foreclosure starts came from loans originated since 2022. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Recently originated loans are driving the current default pipeline , signaling mortgage servicers should be proactive in identifying financial distress. Processing Content Loans originated in 2022 or later accounted for 43% of September's foreclosure starts and 49% of completed sales, according to the September 2026 ICE First Look report. Because new borrowers have accumulated less equity and face higher borrowing costs, servicers should contact borrowers before they become seriously delinquent and find appropriate solutions to prevent foreclosure. "Today's market landscape highlights the value of risk management systems that can seamlessly adapt as the book changes," Andy Walden, head of mortgage and housing market research at ICE, told National Mortgage News. "That means scaling workflows up and down as delinquency volumes shift, spotting borrower stress early, responding quickly and having systems that keep pace with changing loan mix and program requirements with regulatory compliance at the forefront," he added. Loans originated over the last four years accounted for 36% of active mortgages and 40% of loans that were 90 or more days delinquent or in foreclosure, so their share largely reflects market makeup and the distribution of active loans. Lower-credit-score and high-loan-to-value lending accounted for the bulk of struggling loans, with the majority of 2022-2026 vintage defaults coming from borrowers with credit scores below 660 or down payments of 5% or less, Walden said. The report also showed the national delinquency rate increased 12 basis points to 3.66% last month, which was in line with the seasonal norm. The rate remained 34 basis points below September 2019 and less than every other prepandemic September on record. Loans 30 days or more past due rose 5% year over year, while serious delinquencies were up 21% from a year ago. Meanwhile, foreclosure starts decreased 3% on an annual basis last month, completed sales climbed 15% and active foreclosure inventory jumped 37%, its highest level since early 2019, the report found. Prepayment speed also fell to a 19-month low, as single-month mortality declined by four basis points to 0.59%, marking the sixth straight monthly decline from March's 1.06%. Speeds were down 20% annually as mortgage rates, now sitting comfortably above 7% , continue to suppress prepayment activity. "Serious delinquencies and active foreclosures are drawing renewed attention, and they're also where technology makes the most difference," said Bob Hart, president of mortgage technology at ICE, in a press release Tuesday. "Servicers need to reach homeowners early to help keep them in their homes and move quickly from first contact to an executable workout without manual handoffs." Higher energy prices stemming from the Iran war may prove stickier than expected, but the central bank's decision to hold rates steady gives policymakers more time to assess the economic fallout. The dynamic could also lead Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee to consider raising rates at their December meeting in order to bring inflation down to the Fed's 2% target. For now, however, persistent inflation and higher borrowing costs are compounding affordability challenges for many households, economists say. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, said in a post on Oct. 12 that the war has cost the average American household about $2,000 so far, mostly due to higher energy costs, in addition to heightened interest rate costs. "High-net-worth consumers are enjoying the runup in AI stocks and the value of their equity holdings, and are spending with some gusto," Zandi told CNBC. "Lower- and middle-income consumers are increasingly struggling with falling real wages and high rates, and are much more cautious and careful spenders." How the Fed impacts your money The Federal Reserve's decision to keep rates at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, and the expectation that more rate increases are in the pipeline, means consumers are unlikely to see much relief from high borrowing costs anytime soon. The Fed influences the federal funds rate, an interest rate benchmark that sets what banks charge each other for overnight lending. That rate ripples throughout the economy, influencing both consumer borrowing costs and returns on savings. Short-term consumer lending rates, such as credit cards, closely track the prime rate, which typically moves in tandem with the Fed's benchmark and is generally about 3 percentage points higher. Longer-term rates, like those on 30-year mortgages, meanwhile, are driven more by inflation expectations and the economic outlook. items.title: FOMC Leaves Rate Unchanged
items.description: Economic Coverage FOMC Leaves Rate Unchanged By Danielle Hale Oct 28, 2026 The Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee (FOMC), the rate-setting body that meets roughly eight times per year, left the Federal Funds rate unchanged at its October meeting in a target range of 3.75 to 4.0 percent. This hold follows a 25 basis point hike in September, and was supported by 10 of the 12 voting members. Two voters, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, dissented, because they preferred to raise the rate by a quarter percentage point instead of holding. Even though the Fed left its policy rate unchanged in October, the market is anticipating another 2 to 3 hikes over the next 6 to 8 months which would mean a high-end rate range of 4.5 to 4.75 percent. This is slightly above the high-end of Fed funds rate projections made in September, and would position the Fed funds rate roughly halfway between its December 2025 to September 2026 low of 3.5 to 3.75 percent and its 5.25 to 5.5 percent prior peak. While the market and the Fed both seem to agree that some monetary policy restriction is warranted, most investors currently expect more restriction than the Fed has projected. Why further rate hikes are expected Since the September FOMC meeting, when the Fed pushed its rate 25 basis points higher, companies slowed hiring and summer job gains were revised down by 60,000 jobs . The unemployment rate remains relatively stable at 4.2 percent and layoffs are low, but the labor market is less dynamic than is ideal. Meanwhile, inflation surprised to the upside, with the CPI rising 0.6% in September, bringing the annual headline inflation rate to 3.7% as the cost of gas and energy rose sharply. Energy was not the only driver, however, and core CPI, which strips out the cost of food and energy, rose 2.6% in September. Taken together, these indicators suggest that the Fed is likely to continue its focus on inflation, which will likely warrant additional rate hikes. What this means for housing, and homebuyers and sellers Investors have made a round-trip in risk pricing since just before the September Fed meeting. The 10-year yield rose from just under 5 percent to more than 5.3 percent before dipping just under 5 percent in recent days, while mortgage rates climbed from just below 7 percent to more than 7.4 percent. Mortgage rates have not dropped back to their mid-September level, and the housing market is feeling the effects. Pending home sales in September dropped to their lowest level on record according to the National Association of Realtors as buyers and sellers have largely disengaged with the housing market for now. In August and September, existing-home sales dropped below a 4 million sales pace, and are likely to remain low through the rest of the year. Home shoppers shopping in this environment can still set themselves up for a better mortgage rate by boosting their credit, making a higher down payment, and, most importantly, shopping around for a mortgage. Those hoping to make a home purchase in the months ahead should plan for further mortgage rate volatility and rate-proof their home shopping budget by testing out a range of possible mortgage rates so they’ll be prepared to react.

items.title: Homeownership Rate Holds at 65.5% in Q3
items.description: Economic Coverage , Homeownership Homeownership Rate Holds at 65.5% in Q3 By Hannah Jones Oct 28, 2026 2026 Q3 Homeownership and Housing Vacancy Key Takeaways Homeownership rate holds steady. The U.S. homeownership rate was 65.5% in Q3 2026, statistically unchanged from both the prior quarter (65.0%) and a year earlier (65.3%). The rate continues to plateau in a narrow low-to-mid-65% band, with affordability pressures and limited supply showing little sign of easing their grip on the market. Homeowner vacancy remains low and steady. The homeowner vacancy rate held at 1.2% in Q3, virtually unchanged from both the prior quarter and a year earlier. Rental vacancy reaches its highest level in over a decade. The rental vacancy rate rose to 7.6%, up both quarter-over-quarter (7.3%) and year-over-year (7.1%), its highest level since 2014. Renting remains a critical pressure valve, though conditions vary by geography. With a national rental vacancy rate of 7.6%, rental markets continue to offer more flexibility for households unable to buy. Principal cities (8.8%) remain looser than suburbs (6.5%) and non-metro areas (6.4%), which were statistically similar to each other. The South leads in vacancy levels, while the Northeast and West saw the clearest year-over-year shifts. The South posted the highest rental vacancy rate (9.2%) and homeowner vacancy rate (1.5%) of any region, though neither was statistically different from a year ago. Rental vacancy rose significantly in the Northeast (5.0% to 6.2%) and the West (6.0% to 6.7%). Ownership slipped among 35-to-44-year-olds, while older households gained. Homeownership among 35-to-44-year-olds fell from 61.1% to 60.1% year-over-year. Households under 35 remain the lowest at 36.6%, statistically unchanged from 37.5% a year earlier. Meanwhile, 65+ homeownership rose from 77.9% to 79.1%. Racial ownership gaps remain entrenched. Homeownership among Black households fell from 45.7% to 44.4% year-over-year, while White homeownership rose from 74.0% to 75.1%. All other groups did not see statistically significant shifts. What happened this quarter The U.S. homeownership rate held at 65.5% in the third quarter of 2026, statistically unchanged compared with both the prior quarter (65.0%) and a year earlier (65.3%). While the rate remains within the narrow low-to-mid-65% range that has characterized the market in recent years, it continues to run well below the 2020 pandemic-era peak. Mortgage rates pushed back above 7% in late September for the first time in more than a year, which could weigh on would-be buyers heading into the fourth quarter. The homeowner vacancy rate held at 1.2% in Q3 2026, virtually the same as the previous quarter and the previous year. While homeowner vacancy remains below pre-pandemic norms, the recent pick up in inventory could mean vacancy drifts higher if demand is not sufficient to absorb supply. The rental vacancy rate rose to 7.6% in the third quarter, higher than both the previous quarter (7.3%) and the previous year (7.1%). With mortgage rates moving back above 7%, renting continues to stand out as a more affordable alternative to homeownership. However, climbing rental vacancy suggests that units are sitting empty as affordability pressure may discourage household formation. Vacancy was highest in principal cities (8.8%). Suburbs (6.5%) and non-metro areas (6.4%) were lower and not statistically different from each other. Regional differences remain pronounced . The South recorded the highest rental vacancy rate at 9.2%, followed by the Midwest (7.1%), the West (6.7%), and the Northeast (6.2%). The Midwest was higher than the Northeast and statistically similar to the West, while the Northeast and West were not statistically different from each other. Of the four regions, only the Northeast (up from 5.0%) and West (up from 6.0%) saw a statistically significant year-over-year increase in rental vacancy. Rental vacancy has stalled in the South as the wave of supply has subsided . The post-pandemic construction boom flooded these markets with new supply, but as multifamily construction has slowed, vacancy growth has stalled. On the ownership side, the South again led with the highest homeowner vacancy rate at 1.5%, while the other three regions saw vacancy between 0.9% and 1.1%. The Midwest continues to stand out for its high homeownership rate, reaching 69.5% in Q3 2026, though not statistically different from a year earlier, and remains well above the South (67.2%), Northeast (62.9%), and West (60.6%). Different outcomes by race/ethnicity Homeownership rates by race and ethnicity were mixed year over year. In the third quarter, the rate for non-Hispanic White householders rose to 75.1% from 74.0%, while the rate for Asian, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander householders was statistically unchanged at 62.3%. The rate for Black householders fell to 44.4% from 45.7%, and the rate for Hispanic householders was statistically unchanged at 48.1%. The gap between the highest and lowest rates remains more than 30 percentage points, underscoring the persistence of structural barriers to ownership. Different outcomes by age Ownership among younger households remains low, while older householders saw improvement. Homeownership among those under 35 was the lowest of any age group at 36.6%, statistically unchanged from 37.5% a year earlier. Homeownership among households aged 35 to 44 fell from 61.1% in Q3 of 2025 to 60.1% in Q3 of 2026. Ownership in the 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 cohorts held steady at 70.4% and 75.4%, respectively, while the 65+ group saw a 1.2 percentage point improvement to 79.1%. Ample starter-home inventory is crucial for young homeownership, and availability varies significantly across the country .

items.title: Billionaires Fighting California's Wealth Tax Have Put $333 Million Into Political Ad Machine Ahead of Elections
items.description: California's top earners have mobilized and poured more than $300 million into an aggressive public campaign to defeat the controversial Billionaire Tax Act at next week's midterm elections . The measure, which will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot as Proposition 40, would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on the global assets of roughly 200 Californians with a net worth of $1 billion or more who resided in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Championed by a coalition of labor unions, the proposed tax is intended to help fund healthcare for low-income households affected by the the Trump administration's Medicaid cuts. But in the process, it has ignited fierce, bipartisan opposition among California's richest 1%. To eliminate what they view as an existential threat to their business interests, dozens of Silicon Valley billionaires banded together this year to launch Building a Better California , a political action committee. The exceptionally well-funded nonprofit's stated goals include defeating Proposition 40 and, at the same time, supporting two countermeasures. State campaign finance filings reviewed by the New York Times show that roughly 80 deep-pocketed donors, led by Google/Alphabet co-founder Sergey Brin , former Google CEO Eric Schmidt , and prominent investor John Doerr , have spent more than $333 million on the PAC. Brin alone provided $102 million during the first six months of the PAC's existence, before turning off the money spigot and encouraging others to open their wallets. Silicon Valley builds a war chest The tech mogul, whose personal net worth is currently estimated at over $240 billion, according to Forbes, has long been a vocal critic of the billionaire tax. Since the proposal was first introduced, Brin has shifted several Alphabet entities and assets from California to Florida and purchased property in two states: a $51 million Miami megamansion on Florida's Allison Island and a $42 million mansion on the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe . Loading... Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt donated $40 million to the campaign to defeat Proposition 40. Craig Barritt/Getty Images for TIME ; Realtor.com Following in Brin's footsteps, Schmidt and Doerr each contributed $40 million to the cause, followed by Patrick Collison , CEO of Stripe, an online payment processing company, who chipped in $33 million. According to the Times reporting, existing donors to the campaign have been recruiting fellow business leaders to join the fight by contributing cash or stock and becoming actively involved in the PAC. Top venture capitalists, as well as tech entrepreneurs from companies such as DoorDash and Robinhood, have reportedly answered the call. Bipartisan backlash Opposition to the tax extends beyond the tech industry. Outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom , who had tried and failed to keep the proposal off the ballot , has warned that it would lead to an outflow of capital from California, erode the state’s tax base, and stifle innovation with little to show for itself. Loading... California Gov. Gavin Newsom fiercely opposes the proposed billionaire tax and previously tried to defeat it. Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images A large share of the PAC's war chest has funded statewide advertising to urge California voters to reject Proposition 40 and approve the two rival initiatives. Proposition 41 would require audits of new state special taxes, while Proposition 42 would ban new taxes on personal property, including financial portfolios and retirement savings. If both Propositions 40 and 42 pass but the latter captures more votes, it would invalidate the billionaire tax. Beyond traditional TV ads, the campaign has been bombarding voters with anti-Proposition 40 messaging through streaming services, video games such as SimCity, and old-school paper mailers. According to internal documents reviewed by the Times, Building a Better California is committed to delivering a decisive blow to Proposition 40 on Tuesday to "chill wealth-tax efforts nationally." Spending chasm Records reviewed by the Los Angeles Times show that the anti-Proposition 40 camp is outspending its opponents supporting the measure nearly 10 to 1. Proponents of the tax on California's wealthiest residents have raised $34.3 million, primarily from the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which sponsored the ballot measure. However, most of those funds were spent on collecting signatures to qualify the tax proposal for the ballot, leaving the pro-measure camp with just $1.6 million in its coffers as of Oct. 17, according to the L.A. Times. Operating on a shoestring budget, campaigners have been sending voters emails and text messages urging them to embrace Proposition 40 while rejecting Propositions 41 and 42 backed by the Silicon Valley elites. Speaking to the L.A. Times, Suzanne Jimenez , chief of staff of the healthcare union, downplayed the colossal funding gap. "The billionaires think voters are stupid," she told the outlet. "Their spending also makes our case for us. When billionaires can afford to spend millions a day protecting their fortunes, voters can see that billionaires have plenty of money to spare." items.description: An article from Despite pausing rate hikes, ‘inflation is too high’: Fed chair The news didn’t surprise apartment investors, who tuned in for signals indicating future rate increases. Published Oct. 28, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images As expected, the Federal Open Market Committee held interest rates steady on Wednesday, following its two-day October meeting. Despite two dissenters who voted to raise the federal funds rate target range by 0.25 percentage points, the FOMC kept it at 3.75% to 4%. For the apartment industry, the news was welcome after the FOMC hiked the federal funds rate target range by 25 basis points in September. “Expectations are clearly for the Fed to stand pat, which helps,” Jeff Brown, CEO and co-founder at T2 Capital Management, told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments ahead of the Fed’s announcement. In a press conference following today's announcement, Kevin Warsh, chair of the Federal Reserve, said the goal was to deliver price stability. He also announced a change to the Fed’s 2028 schedule. It will still meet eight times, but only six will set policy. “As we widen the frame to survey the broad economic and financial picture, real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction,” Warsh said. “That's good news. But inflation is too high.” Multiple multifamily owners and investors said they would watch the announcement closely, even if they don’t expect relief anytime soon. Instead, they wanted to understand what could be coming late in the year and in 2027. Trickle-down effect After multiple rate cuts in 2025 , the Fed held rates steady before raising them in September, a move that affected the multifamily market. While “cap rates have moved out since the September meeting,” sellers are slow to accept it, said Tyler Chesser, the co-founder and managing partner of CF Capital. “Historically it takes a few quarters for seller expectations to catch up to the market,” Chesser said. “Until they do, the bid-ask gap means a lot of deals stall, get retraded, or die. I’d expect volume to stay thin through year-end, especially if the Fed signals a December hike.” Smita Garg, principal of investments and asset management at apartment owner and manager SKG Capital, said her firm was closely watching the Fed’s announcement because it “was actively evaluating and executing transactions where today’s cost of capital has a direct impact on pricing and returns.” “Higher borrowing costs continue to make multifamily transactions more difficult to execute,” Garg told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. “Financing costs directly affect what buyers can pay while still achieving appropriate returns, and sellers have not always adjusted expectations to the same degree. That disconnect continues to limit transaction volume.” Forward outlook In its statement, the Federal Reserve said economic activity is expanding at a strong pace, and domestic spending has been resilient, despite geopolitical uncertainty. “Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust,” Warsh said. “Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.” Financial and credit conditions have tightened for some businesses and households after September’s rate hike, according to Warsh. “Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations, and while overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight,” Warsh said. “But broadly, these developments go in the direction of achieving a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.” Still, Warsh said multiple times that inflation remains elevated. “Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored,” he said. Warsh said more information is needed before the Fed decides to raise rates again, noting that indicators like oil futures were continuing to rise. “Ensuring price stability … quashing inflation, is not about some fixed individual date on a calendar,” Warsh said. “[The] same way, it's not about some isolated data point.” Tone matters For apartment observers, Warsh’s comments seemed to matter more than the Fed’s decision. Chesser wasn’t surprised by the rate pause, but he wanted to know what comes later. “After September’s hike, the market is trying to read whether another one comes in December, and Chair Warsh’s tone will move the 10-year Treasury more than the decision itself,” Chesser said. “That matters for us because most apartment debt is priced off Treasuries, not the Fed funds rate.” Like Chesser, Garg was also watching Wednesday’s announcement to decipher the Fed’s roadmap into 2027. “For us, the more important question is not necessarily this week’s decision, but the direction of rates over the next six to 12 months,” Garg said. “Greater visibility around the rate path would help bring more certainty back to underwriting and ultimately help buyers and sellers close the gap on pricing.” Regardless, some firms are preparing for higher rates to stick around. “I don't know that we're going to see material drops in rates over the near term,” Greg Cavanaugh, senior vice president of development for the mid-Atlantic region at Bainbridge, told Multifamily Dive. Even with Wednesday’s announcement and Warsh's comments, Chris Nebenzahl, CBRE's Americas head of multifamily research, said the market might not have a clear picture for a few more months. "Greater clarity around the rate outlook should materialize in early 2027, helping bring buyers and sellers back together, improving price discovery and supporting higher transaction volume as investors gain confidence in the market,” he said in emailed comments. items.title: Down Payment Assistance Could Cut the Time to Save for a Home by a Year and a Half or More
items.description: Down Payment Assistance Could Cut the Time to Save for a Home by a Year and a Half or More Nationally, a 3.5% down payment boost allows a typical buyer to save for a 10% down payment 35% faster October 28, 2026 Anushna Prakash Written by Anushna Prakash Key findings: A median-income household could save 10% down on the typical U.S. home after 4.2 years, according to Zillow’s estimates. With down payment assistance covering 3.5% of that, the time to save would be cut to 2.7 years. Moving from a 6.5% down payment to 10% on a typical U.S. home would save a buyer $1,080 per year in monthly payments. Nationally, those monthly savings would bring an additional 26,338 homes within reach for a median-income buyer. Saving 10% down on the typical U.S. home takes the median household an estimated 4.2 years, or about four years and two months. With a down payment assistance program covering 3.5% of that 10% down payment, the same household could have enough saved a year and a half sooner. The same assistance also lowers a typical buyer’s mortgage payments by $1,080 a year, putting more homes within reach. Nationally, about 26,300 more active listings would become affordable in this scenario. For this analysis, Zillow is assuming a buyer puts a total of 10% down and receives an FHA loan . However, the minimum down payment for an FHA loan is 3.5%, meaning a buyer could also use this level of assistance to cover the entirety of their down payment. Making a smaller down payment does bring up the monthly mortgage payment some, but is a viable option for a buyer with the financial means to cover the monthly payment but without the necessary savings for a down payment. Zillow research has shown that one in five renter households headed by someone ages 29 to 43 could afford the monthly cost of owning a typical home in their market with just 5% down. A 3.5% boost cuts the time to save a 10% down payment by as much as 3.2 years Nationally, a median-income household saving for a 10% down payment on a typical U.S. home needs 4.2 years. That number could be cut to 2.7 years with a 3.5% boost from down payment assistance, a difference of 1.5 years. The benefit is biggest for a buyer in some of the most expensive metro areas, led by Los Angeles, where the years to save fall from 9.1 years to 5.9 years, putting homeownership within reach more than three years sooner. Three other major California metros see gaps of more than two and a half years: San Jose (8.5 years to 5.5 years with down payment assistance), San Diego (7.9 to 5.1) and San Francisco (7.7 to 5). Pittsburgh is the only major metro area where down payment assistance does not shave at least a year off the time needed to save 10% down on a typical home. A median-income Pittsburgh household could save 10% down after 2.7 years, which would be shortened to 1.8 years with down payment assistance. Lower payments save buyers $1,080 a year, bringing more listings within budget With a 6.5% down payment and a 6.78% mortgage rate (the average rate for an FHA loan in September), the monthly payment on a $366,157 home (the typical home value in September, according to the Zillow Home Value Index) would have been $3,010, including estimates for taxes, insurance and maintenance. If given a 3.5% boost via down payment assistance, that same home purchase would come with a monthly payment of $2,920, a savings of $1,080 per year. The annual savings are largest in San Jose ($4,608), San Francisco ($3,396), Los Angeles ($2,880), San Diego ($2,808) and New York ($2,160). Those monthly payment savings can bring more homes within reach. Nationally, 359,434 active listings were affordable to this hypothetical buyer with 6.5% down in September, representing 25.7% of what was listed for sale. With the 3.5% down payment assistance, 26,338 more listings would have been affordable, raising the share of affordable listings to 27.6%. Receiving 3.5% in down payment assistance would have brought the most listings newly within reach in Dallas (864), Atlanta (712), Miami (558) and Washington, D.C. (555). How the numbers work For years-to-save calculations , Zillow assumes a median-income household saves 10% of its income each month. This analysis assumes a household is buying the typical home in a given metro, as measured by the Zillow Home Value Index as of September 2026 .
